blocks.x: That's the gang he was with when he married me. That's the gang he was with when he married me. When were you married? Do you remember the year? Do I? He married me in 1922. 1922? He was playing with the Eureka then. He was playing then.
You know when that picture was taken with the little boys?

That's what I'm trying to find. How long ago? Was that when you first married him? Oh, he had that when I married him. Oh, Lord, I don't know nothing about that. He had that before I married him, but I wish I could find that little picture. So y'all could see it.
I sure would like to know who has the music.

With some of his music. Now I couldn't tell you so many different ones come. Some of them dead would come there and guide him. If I know it all or something was coming along, I'd have kept it all. But you know how it is when people beg you for something? Yeah, you can't keep everything. No, I couldn't keep them. And then I had to move from where I was on Bonita Street because the house comes to leaking, you see. And that made me have to move. Well, I had to move when I had to move, you see. I was wondering who his teacher was. Did he ever tell you what he was? Uh-uh. He never did tell me. He must have had one. He had a teacher. The Lord, he had them. He had some knowledge, alright. And he could read the notes and everything. He was like, oh, you know what he was doing? I was wondering who his teacher was. Did he ever tell you what he was?

Uh-uh. He never did tell me. He must have had one. He had a teacher. The Lord, he had them. He had some knowledge, alright. And he could read the notes and everything. He was like, oh, you know what he was doing? He had some knowledge, alright.
And he could read the notes and everything just as good as he could. He sure could read the notes. He must have had somebody to learn him, you know. He couldn't learn by himself. He had to learn.
He said he could make arrangements. He had the cards in there, right?

Yeah, he had cards. He fixed them cards his shop, you know. Fixed all that. Oh, God, you ought to see him with that thing up on his shoulder. The child was just particularly like that. If he was fixing, he'd go sit down and eat a meal. And I had to wash that bag, you know, and keep it clean. And he stick all that down there. He had a little thing on the side where he stick the oil for the put on his horn. Then he had two mouthpieces and he made, I had bags I made. Now in the wintertime I had to heat them on the fire. Now after he take them off the fire, he stick them where it stay warm. But you see, he changed the mouthpiece. You see, I couldn't sell the mouthpiece. I had to throw them away. And he paid extra for them mouthpieces. I'd like to have it myself.
You should have saved those. Those are still good.

Well, the mouthpieces, all that was good. He paid four and a half for them. Some guy more than you. And the horn would cost plenty money too. Oh, yeah. Don't you think he didn't pay plenty for his horn? I don't know. I had it the other day. I was looking at it and I said, I had it. And what I done with it, I don't know. Is it in that box? Yeah, that's the box it was in.
Well, we can look through it again. One by one. I'm looking through it.
I don't know where. I don't know where.
I think I'd know it if I'd see it too.
Oh, I know it. He got two little bars with it.
Yeah, I remember that part. Did they have much music in Biloxi when you were young?

When I was young? Not nothing much. I used to go there and play what you're talking about. I played big parades. Yeah. With the old fellows. You know, the paint rocks and all them. You know, he used to go all over there with them.
Did he go there before you knew him? Did he say that?
Oh, yeah. He had been going over there before he knew me.
Mm-hmm.
My sister got acquainted with him, you see, after he was married to me. My sister used to fix the dinner for him when they come over there, fix their dinners for all of them. Mm-hmm. Yeah.
Did you say Dr. Bichet had five pictures of yours or just that one?
No, it was the picture of Willie.
Oh, the whole band.

Yeah, the band. That's what it was, and I didn't want to get rid of it. It had Willie. Willie was standing over the slide, and Buddy Bowden, and all of them. But I didn't get it back, and I often wondered what to come up. And I went down there, and we hunted, we hunted. Nobody knowed him. Mm-hmm. But I had that dress, you understand?
Yeah, it was right there, 1400 St. Bernard.
That's right, yeah, in the 1400s.
Right there at the corner.

Well, he wasn't there no more. I ain't know the man died until you told me. Well, that's what happened. Yeah, I said that to you. Oh, and it wasn't good. He saw it. It was good, wasn't it? Yes. Yeah. I was gonna have it in, uh, large, you know, from that. Then I was gonna get a frame, you understand? And put it in the frame. I said, well, I'd keep that. I'd say, maybe someday somebody may come along, and they would want that, and it might be something to them, you know? And so many people done asked me for that little picture. Yeah.
Well, we'll check it and see if we can't find a copy of it.

I wish to God I could get it. I sure wish I could get it, because it was a good picture. He saw it, because it was the one I showed it to. Yeah, you was the one I showed it to, because it's not recognized.
Yeah, I have a copy in that book. Yeah, it is. I know I'd find it.
Hold me. Hold me.
Let me see what I did after all these times. Lord, all that time.
Well, that's a good picture, too. It's a good picture of him.
Real clear. He wasn't, he didn't weigh 260 pounds then, though, did he?
Oh, no, he got me. I have his picture in here, where I had his picture, you know, in the bedroom.
Oh, can I help you with that?

Yeah, this is his picture. This cost me $14. A man down there fixed this for me. That's all I had. So that's a great big one. That wasn't taken. Was that taken from here? Yes, sir. He took five of them. Then he sent me a letter, and he told me to come, and I went down there, and he kept one, way down on Roy Street. Now, and I picked that. And then he fixed that frame that made it show up, and everybody says it's like him.
Well, this gives all about his company. That's nice. Did you want to read that out? Yeah.
Everybody says it's like him.
Let me read this. It says, Role of Honor, World's Great War for Freedom.
I know I would find it.
World's Great War for Freedom. United we stand. It looks like it has an American flag and an English flag.
The Spanish American flag. Oh, that's the Spanish flag. The Spanish American flag is yellow. See, I know.
It says, W.M. Cornish. Company F. Regiment 9th U.S. VOL. I guess that's Volunteer.
Volunteer.
Infantry INF.

Yeah. Yeah. It's a reason that the man didn't write it all on there like he should have. I had it on another piece of paper somewhere. Let me see. Somewhere else I had it. The man didn't fix it correctly. He fixed it like that. I said, well, Benzie, fix it like that. I'm going to carry it home. I ain't going to say no more to the man because he might mess it up.
That's right.
Yeah, some of them mess it up. That's the picture I showed you. Isn't it? Yeah.
Mm-hmm. That's right.
Yeah, that's the picture I showed him. Huh?
That's the other one. It's the one I saw.
That's the picture I showed him.
Yeah, that's the same picture though.
And then you've seen the picture of the other consigned too where the man down in St. Bernard. That's the one. I'd give anything to get that.
It says, uh, place of enlistment NOLA. New Orleans, Louisiana.
Mm-hmm.
Date of enlistment July 22nd, 1898. Camp Corbin, Louisiana.
See, this is what I took to get the money off him. Oh my God, I like to woe out.
Oh, that's...
That's what I took to get the money off him. I woe out. The man woe me out going there. He woe me out. And I wrote that down myself, you know. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
It says served two years. Mm-hmm. You better read all this in case some of this might be different because I've checked that.
The man didn't fix it right on there like he should have. Like I told him. He didn't fix it all on there. Because the man figured... He got paid for it, but he didn't fix it. You understand?
Is this an XC-2-3-7-3-1-3-1? Yeah. That was a long one. Mm-hmm. Might be XG-2-3-7-3. What do you mean this year?
Yeah. Oh no, that's a XG. And that's a 2 and that's a 3-7-3-1-3-1.

Oh my husband said when he went to war, he told me he went on the Philippine island. He went all out in Cubial. He went to all them places and lived on the island and everything. Could he ask me? Oh my God, when they asked me that up there where I went to the vet and be... I stayed there so long until I just got sick. They sure can ask you some questions. Mm-hmm. Oh, I went for three solid weeks every other day. And every time I go, I'd get a new number. First time I went, I got 21. Next time I went, they gave me number 2. Next time I went, I had number 39. Sometime I'd be coming home way late, even 3 o'clock. Sometime 4 o'clock. And we'd be packing. And some of them women, they couldn't tell you when their husband died. And couldn't tell you when they got married. He said, well, what kind of women is y'all? Why they call it? He told them that. Well, you tell me you don't know when you married a man. Wasn't that foolish?
Yeah.

And he just looked at me. He said, where you come from? I said, Bluxy. He said, you went to school? I said, I went to ninth grade and I walked a whole mile with Brogan shoes on, bravest tips. And he just looked at me. He said, well, you... He said, your education is pretty good. I went to ninth grade and I wanted to go to college. When my mother died and left my dad was 16th year old, that made me and my biggest sister had to work. But don't you think we don't know how to read and write and figure? I know if I... And I know some girls right now, white girls, where I used to work at, they'd go to college and they'd come in my bedroom at night and I said, Bella, I said, what? Show me how to do this. I said, well, y'all going to college? And they don't know good as me and you know. That's true, ain't it? Yeah. They don't know good as you. Because, see, when we went to school, we had the lawn. Now when they go to school, they exercise us and all that. We didn't do that. We went to school. We stayed in there. Twelve o'clock we come out and we eat us lunch. We go back in for one o'clock. And three o'clock, my papa be right there with the wagon and the horse to get us. You hear me? And don't you think we sat up in that kitchen that night in that dining room and he sat there with a trap. And he made us study that lesson. He said, y'all didn't grow up here. And I see some girls come up with, when I come up, they don't know how to hear from a V. Right there. Get into college, they can hardly read. Miss Neal would tell me get letters, they come in. Boom, boom, boom, boom. Miss Bella read my letter. Ain't that's pitiful? Oh, I think that's pitiful. For people that have to, you know, read.
Well, some people didn't get the chance though. Some people didn't have the chance to go to school.

Well, I didn't want to go to school. My papa beat me and made me go. Now I'm glad today I went. I didn't want to go. Oh, that lesson was hard. We had the McGuffey's books and the McGuffey's spellers. They don't have that no more. I've seen them though. My mother saved her. Oh, oh, oh. I had two I saved. They over the lake against my sister and them guys. Oh, them things was hard to spell. And they put, put about that much on the blank book. Put numbers. From there, way down to there and then they draw that line.
Those old spellers.

Now you had that to count up and you better have it straight. If you didn't, they stand you to the board and make you write your name like my name was Isabella. They make me write a hundred times and I look at the teacher. She said, now you write on that side. I said, I said, how many? She said, write clean till your daddy come. And then when my daddy come again, we go home, my papa whoop him. Cause I had right to know it. See?
I better give you this back. Cause you don't want to lose that either. Can I help you put it up?
Yeah, I'll put it back. It's alright, ain't it?
Oh, that's nice.

Yeah. Now a lot of people in my gang, they come to my house and say, Bella, where'd you get that? Now they don't have their husband's picture where he was in his pantry anymore. But I keep that. That cost me $15, but I don't mind it. But that's all I had of him. But that's just like him. Yeah, cause he was kind of rough looking in the face. You know, his face wasn't real smooth like some people. But he was nice. You see? He had nice ways and he got by anyways he went too. Don't you think he did?
Can you reach that alright? Oh, yeah.

You don't want me to help you? No, I can put that up there. This is nice. Good job there. Don't you worry. I'm used to taking it down, cleaning all around it and putting that up. When I was on Medina Street, I was supposed to have it by the front door, they told me. And somebody come to my house and they let the front door open and the wind blowed in it and broke the glass. So it cost me $5 per glass. I said, now wherever I go now, I'll put them on the mantel feet. You see the door open and that wind. Yeah, and it broke it. You know, huh?
You don't smoke, do you?
Oh, that's a habit I haven't got. Oh, well you're lucky.
You're lucky.
Huh?
You're lucky.
Yeah. I don't smoke.
Uh, was your husband born here in the city?

Uh-uh. Born up in Carlton, but I don't know where I am. And, uh... Born and raised, because you see when they got ready to put me on the pension, pension they went to the scenery, what do you call that? And they found out where he was born. I told them he was born up in Carlton, but they found out where it was at. See, they find all that out there self. Yeah, because I know he was born up there, but his mama told me he was born up in Carlton, because she told me he was 16 years old when his daddy died. She told me that, his mother. Uh-huh. He was 16 years old when he found it. But you see, some white people wanted my husband to be a prize fighter, because he was double-jointed. Boy, he was so big. You never seen him? No, they forgot to see him, you know. Now, the gentlemen would fix them books. They saw him. Yes, I know. Oh, they stayed there and talked to him. They said he was a sensible man. They had about three or four pages they took away from my house. They sat there and talked to him. He could talk then, you know, but he was in the bed pile on. They helped me to set him up in the bed, and we put the pillows behind him. And they said he was a sensible man for to be sick, and he was sick, and I didn't worry. Like some men, you know, would worry. And they sat there nearly a half a day. They said they never saw a man like him. That's when they made that book. Oh, they got plenty from him, because he knowed about Buddy Bowling, and he knowed a lot of it, and Lord, he was just tickled to death. Yeah. They got all that out of it.
Was he there at home on Perdido Street at that time?

Mm-hmm. 20, 24, Padida. I used to live. Mm-hmm. That's where I showed you that little picture, what I showed you. Yeah. Mm-hmm. But that's all the pictures I got of him. When him and I got married, we went to the studio, and they had the picture taken. I had two took, and then I kept one. Somebody stole it when he was sick, when me and him got married. And the bridesmaid took it, and then she died, and I guess her husband throwed that away, because people don't keep pictures. No. But it's nice to keep them. It's nice to keep it.
Yeah. That's the only picture of that band that we've ever seen, that one that your husband had.
Wasn't that Piddler?
With Buddy Bowling.
I wouldn't mind y'all could search y'all, and they would go down there and find me.
We'll try to. We'll try to find these things.
Because you see, I would have that right there now to show it to y'all if it wasn't for that, the gentleman.
That's what Dr. Shae's wife might have it.

Somebody died. I said one day I was going to go down there and inquire for him. He gave me that, and he told me, he told me, don't come under a month. But when the month was up, I went. I said, now I done give that man that nice picture. And Willie told me he was the oldest one, had one left, said all of them had one when they all come in dying out. And he said when they took Buddy Bowling, when they put him in the crazy house, he died, you know. He died in the crazy house.
Did you ever hear your husband say anything about making a record with that band?

Never did. Never did. But I guess if he lived, he would have. Yeah, because he had good opportunity. If he lived, he'd have made records. It was a good band, I'm telling you. Warner and all of them can tell you. Y'all say you've been to Warner. Warner played with him a long time too. I don't know how long, but Warner was playing with him. Warner was playing with him when he fell sick. But Warner used to come to my house all the time to see about it.
Did you ever know King Oliver by any chance?
No, I've heard talk of him. Joe Oliver, they called him around here.
Yeah, yeah.
He's a carnet player.

He's in Chicago, eh? He died. He died during Chicago, yeah. Some place. Some place out there, yeah. I've heard people spoke. I've heard my husband talk about him and all, but for me knowing him, I didn't know him.
I just wondered if your husband ever mentioned playing with various fellows. No.

But I believe my husband played with all of them, to tell the truth. My husband used to play in the Tuxedo Band and all of them. I guess John and them could tell you that. He used to play with any of them, for that's concerned. And then when he had that band, what they played in. Because they used to come get him, you know, he'd go play with any of them. Money wasn't worth money then. Yeah. And then they made good.
Which Tuxedo was that he played with? With Papa Celestan or with John?
Oh, Papa Celestan, he was good buddies. He used to play with all of them. He played with all of them. I don't believe he played with John. No, he was sick when John took that band over, I think.
Did they ever travel around very much? You mentioned they went to Biloxi.
Yeah, he went to Biloxi, I know.
Did they ever go to Texas or anything?

I don't know. He went different places before he was with me. Because Mama told me he used to always be gone with different bands, different places. But you see, I wasn't with him at the time. That's the trouble. You see. Men used to come get him at the house there and I wouldn't see him no more. Wouldn't even see him no more. He'd be gone. You see, he was busy, you know. He made the living with him. I guess he was trying to catch every way he could catch, you know. Oh, he had plenty of places he played for loads of people. Yes, indeed.
Do you remember anything else about Bob Lyons? He's dead now, but I thought we won't get to talk to him, of course. I wondered if you knew anything about his life.

No, I couldn't tell you nothing about Bob Lyons. All I know he used to be with Willie there, you know, play with him and all. But for me to have anything to say of him, I wouldn't know. I know he didn't worry with him too much, you know. My husband and them would be together with him. All the musicians used to be around there by Ruchacks. And used to be around there by Johnny Matoyas, where he's dead. You heard of him, eh? Certainly. When he died, Johnny Matoyas, he died. But he used to be there, because that's where them Zulus used to meet and that's where Willie and them used to play. Willie and them used to play for him. Warner could tell you that too, you know. He told you?
Where is Matoyas' place? He's all towed down.

He's all towed down there. Oh yeah, well that's where my husband and them used to go and they would play. They'd leave the horns all in my house, on the bed. Then they'd all go around there. When they'd get ready to start off playing, they'd all come back and get their horns. That was by Johnny Matoyas. He used to stay there, you see. That was where the Zulus used to have their meetings. Then they used to meet there.
Was that in the Air Ramport?

That was right in the block where Root Shack was on Padilla Street. Oh yeah, the same? Yeah, on the same side. Because, let me see, Root Shack was on the corner. And Johnny, and then they had a little, that cook shop like you say. And then Johnny Matoyas was right next door to that. But all that's towed down, that whole thing. So I'm going to go out there and get lost. I could get well now.
I think that Zulu is still in the pavement. The sidewalk still says Zulu Aid and Pages.

Yeah, yeah, and I just fixed it and said the pavement. Well, that's where the Zulus was, right there. All of them used to go there. I have a picture of that place. Yeah, all of them used to go there. Well, my husband and them had their band. They used to be white people come from the north and take their band, take my husband and them's pictures, you know, in the band. Yeah, they used to take it and carry it. Last time I went out there, I had some children. I was mining for a lady. And the lady asked me, oh, she said, where is the big man? Used to play the sliding trampone and went, ooh, that woman filled me up. I said, who are you? She said, I'm talking to you, lady. I said, oh, he died. Oh, she said, that band ain't like it used to be when he played. Show you the difference how she could tell, eh? Well, he was the one done the playing, you see, the slide. The slide was the one that would start off, you know. That's why. Right up in front. Well, he'd be in the front of him and Warner, and they would start the playing, you see. And when they start the playing, then the others would come right on in. And show you how she knows. She said, well, the other players said, we come with on here. She said, oh, we want to take the pitch. Oh, she said, the Zulus ain't like it used to be. I said, no, ma'am. I said, well, that big man, he's dead. That's my husband. She said, oh. She said, what a pity. And I'll show you how they noticed things. Oh, he's a good player. You got to give it to him. Yes, ma'am. They had a good band. And you could tell that band anywhere. I could be in my house, and I could tell that band anywhere. It could be four, five, six blocks. I could tell that band when they be coming. You could tell it. But just now it was good. I could tell them. Oh, they ain't like that no more. Uh-uh.
What happened during the Depression?
Did he still continue on playing in it?
Who, Miles? Yeah. So I used to play when the Depression was, but they didn't get as much music to play, you know, as they did before. But they'd get some, but not as half as much, you know.
I just wondered if he got a job with one of those government bands, you know.

No, I don't know who he used to be. He come get his horn going out, I wouldn't know where he's going. You just tell him I'm going to play, Bella, and that's all. He didn't have much to say. He was unconcerned. You never see him laugh. He was always, uh, in earnest. You know what he had to do. Like some of them, they would laugh. He never did much, wasn't much, when he laughed it would be a surprise. I said, Lord, the man don't even laugh to myself. He never knew he was in earnest with that horn. And when somebody would hire him and all that was his mind on that. He knew he was making his, well, making his living. You couldn't blame him for that, could you? He was making his living. I used to look at him. His mama told me, said, Bella, he'll never laugh. And he'll sit down and he'll sit down and he wouldn't have hardly, nothing to say. And sometimes I say, Willie, so and so. He said, uh-huh, that's all. He wouldn't have nothing to say to you? I used to look at him. I said, well, what kind of man is he? His mama said, Bella, he's done by nothing but that music. She told me, she said, you're wasting time talking to Willie. I said, Willie, talking about that music. And when they say music, he's gone.
Oh, that's what he was.

A person interested in anything, you know how they is. Everybody's like that. He sure they like music. And he's missing, too, because they say so. They tell me. Lots of people tell me. I met a man the other day. He said, y'all can see. When they see the bands and I said, Lord, for Willie, sure he's missing this bell. He said, we can tell. And yet, they had a parade a couple of months ago, it was, and I seen some of them. He was on the corner and I seen some of the men on that side, and I went down there where they was. They talked to them, some of them. And they said, oh, Bella, look a corner. He said, Bella, we showed him Miss Willie. I said, y'all miss him? I said, well, I miss him, too. He said, yeah, well, we miss Willie. Yes, indeed. And when they go to play, he wouldn't know how to come get him. Don't you think they would? Come on, Willie, you go and say, yeah, I'm coming.
Did they have a parade about every week, every Sunday?

Well, sometimes every Sunday mostly they used to parade, big parade. They used to play for them. You see, like, how do you call it? Like, in May, you know, the second Sunday in May. The odd fellas. Oh, Captain Darcy. You know Captain Darcy?
Mm-hmm, I believe so.

Well, he wouldn't get no, he looked like a white man. He wouldn't get nobody with Willie. Come to my house two o'clock in the morning. That must be Eddie, I think, huh? He got a sister there across the street, but he lived down on Denver Street somewhere.
He's a bass player, too, isn't he?

No, he didn't play music at all. He just was, he's a Mason. And he would just come high Willie. He went high Willie, he would, for the band. Oh, he'd come get it paid out on, put on the such a bottom one to keep Willie. Yeah. And he used to play for them women, them Bill-ranked women, you know, all when they drill in the street, and they make letters with themselves. Oh, yeah. And they make letters with themselves. I used to play for all them, you know, it must have been good to do that. Had to.
I never saw them make letters in the street. You saw them?
You never saw it? It's something pretty, yeah, they could make the letters.
Some of the ladies in the Elks organization do that sometimes. I mean, they could go and- Yeah, they make letters. March, big march around in circles and different things. Yeah.

Well, the Patriots, my husband used to be with, would play with, and Captain Dawson, and they had them women, the number seven drill rank, and the women. They really made letters with themselves. I don't know how they could do it. They formed the letter. Make letters. I guess they just, they done a practice, they self-ture it. They make them letters. It was something to look at, I'm telling them.
Sure was.
Did Mr. Carnish ever have any pupils that come to the house after you married him? Any pupil that learned trombone from you?
No, just them boys used to come there, but them boys with good sizes used to come there with you boys, but I don't know where they went. I don't know where they went.
And he had this picture when you were married then already?

Already, yeah. He had it pasted on something, and I tore it off, and I said, I'm going to get a picture taken. He said, don't have my picture taken. And I used to beg him to have his picture taken, you know, with his band suit on. I said, why don't you have your picture taken? I said, I don't want to buy my picture. His mama say always, and his mother never had a picture of herself, old as she was. Can you beat that? She was 105. 105 from the way we counted when he died. I have my picture. What? But I had it taken.
How old was his father when he died?
Oh, I don't know. His father was in the Spanish and in the Civil War.
The Civil War, yeah.
Now that's my picture. I had that taken.
Well, that's nice.

I've had it a good while ago. Yeah, the man who took it, he kept one. He said, I took a good picture. Well, if I put in the, if I dress up, I don't make a nice picture. But if I just put on something plain, I make, yeah. I had 12 of them tooken. And I carried lots of them away to different places and give them to my kinfolks and sent them for Easter. Yeah, everybody says, it's just like me.
Yeah.
Yeah. And I kept that and I said I was going to have it enlarging, you know.
You still look about that way since 70 years old.

Yeah, I'm 70 years old now. Yeah. Maybe when you see me dressed up, I don't look like this, though. I have a cape. I got regular military outfits, you know, put on white uniforms and everything. I took some flags. I have a uniform, a cap, a flower. We dress just like, like American flags.
You have a flower that you're saying?
Well, they have a flower we put some.
Ha!
Come through this away. That's alright. Where you at?
